title: What Does Learning Looks Like in Action -5
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton describes the fourth and worst learning state, drowning, using his wife's disastrous move from easy ski slopes onto a black run before her skills were consolidated. The brain's response to a huge gap between what is hardwired and what is demanded is panic, helplessness and a wish to quit, and what then becomes sticky is the helplessness itself. He argues that drowning can be hidden by learners who feel shame, so teachers must look for quieter signs such as worried expressions, avoided eye contact and borrowed answers. A personal Duolingo episode shows that dropping back into easy practice (treading water) can rescue a learner and restore confidence. The goal stated is to maximise new and consolidating good struggle, minimise treading water and eliminate bad struggle, and he asks readers for a better word than drowning.
points: Drowning occurs when the gap between what is hardwired and what is now demanded is too large, and the learner can end up learning helplessness instead of the content.
Learners often hide drowning out of shame, so teachers need to check on subtle signs rather than wait for tears or refusal.
Moving a learner onto harder material before skills are consolidated invites exactly the collapse Jean experienced on the mountain.
Returning to easy practice can rescue a drowning learner, which gives treading water an occasional legitimate role.
quotes: Bad struggling happens when we are way out of our comfort zone, when we don't really know what we are doing, when we are getting worse rather than better and when our motivation to keep going just disappears.

Jean fell within twenty metres of starting the black run and everything that might have been even partly sticky just drained away. Nothing worked, and the less it worked the more her brain used up all its energy on generating fear and embarrassment.

When we are faced with a real mismatch between what we have already hardwired (or not) and what we now need to be able to know or do, drowning occurs to all of us in our lives. Many people have a debilitating fear of public speaking, of dancing in public, of having to cook a complex meal, of having to lead a team into uncharted areas, of walking into a party at which they know no-one. All of these can induce the state of drowning.

Of course, this doesn’t stop some learning happening, because the brain is always on. When we are repeatedly in the deep end of this horrible drowning situation, what we learn - what we consolidate through our powerful Drowning experiences - is not what we are supposed to learn, but our helplessness. We learn to not want to learn any more.

But many of us - children and adults together - hide these feelings of incompetence and our unwillingness to learn from others. We don’t want our peers to make fun of us. We don’t want to reveal our lack of ability.
Drowning learners take a double hit. Not only do they not learn what was planned for them to learn, they also learn feelings and emotions about their learning that will be unhelpful going forward.

Reverting to treading water rescued me from drowning just like my swimming teacher said it might. It can be the strategy to help our children and students, too. But the truth is that, as much as possible, we want to maximise our students’ new and consolidating good struggling, minimise their treading water no struggling and eliminate the bad struggling whenever we can.
